look_here_first: START WITH THE FINGERLIKE FLOWERING BRANCHES: several narrow, one-sided racemes (commonly 3–7 in the Williamson County treatment) cluster near the culm tip, each holding PAIRED stalked spikelets on one side of a flattened/winged branch. It is a spreading, usually annual grass with roots at prostrate nodes and a distinct translucent MEMBRANOUS ligule around 1–3 mm. Distinguish large crabgrass using magnified sterile lemma nerves, not general hairiness.

best_field_traits: Annual or short-lived plant with sprawling, decumbent lower stems that can root at nodes, often forming patches.
Terminal seedhead with several roughly fingerlike, often subdigitate one-sided flowering racemes, commonly about 3–7, though counts vary.
Paired stalked spikelets on the underside/one side of a narrow, somewhat winged branch (rachis); paired spikelets and unequal stalks can be resolved with a macro.
Leaf blades frequently about 5–9 mm wide in Central Texas treatments; longer basal blade hairs may occur, so grass hairiness alone is not a species key.
TRUE ligule a whitish, semitranslucent MEMBRANE around 1–3(–4) mm long, often irregularly jagged at top. Confirm at the sheath–blade joint.
Very small lower glume and longer upper glume accompany two-flowered spikelets with a sterile lower and fertile upper floret.
Sterile lower lemma lateral nerves tend to be smooth or only sparsely prickly in this taxon; need 10–20× examination to distinguish some other crabgrass species.
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Large crabgrass (D. sanguinalis) has more prickles on the sterile lemma lateral veins, often with hairier upper leaves. Smooth crabgrass (D. ischaemum) usually has smaller spikelets. Goosegrass (Eleusine indica) has a flattened whitish crown and dense, zipperlike rows of spikelets.
crew_field_check: Photograph whole plant, stem/roots, whole seedhead and single spikelet from same mature individual.
Use panicle architecture FIRST; confirm true ligule and spikelet anatomy only with proper scale.
Never annotate a structural feature that is not physically resolvable in the source photo.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Plant-level photo showing decumbent spreading stems and rooted nodes (if visible) with scale.
Overhead intact flowerhead with count of fingerlike racemes.
Macro of one flowering branch showing two spikelets per rachis node, unequal stalk lengths and branch winging.
Blade–sheath collar with 1–3 mm transparent true ligule and mm ruler.
Mature spikelet lifted with a fine tool; compare upper glume and sterile lemma lateral nerve prickles at 10–20×.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Fall witchgrass (D. cognata) has a broad, OPEN, very airy broom/tumbleweed panicle with branching wiry stems and solitary tiny spikelets at slender twig tips, frequently with long conspicuous hairs around swollen branch bases; it is a perennial, not a flat-fingered patch. Large crabgrass (D. sanguinalis) may be nearly identical in gross shape: inspect lateral nerves of the sterile lemma under magnification; that taxon tends to have more pronounced prickles. Smooth crabgrass (D. ischaemum) often has smaller spikelets. Goosegrass (Eleusine indica) shows very flat whitish stems and densely zipperlike multi-spikelet rows, not the Digitaria paired spikelets.
